dedupe_keys.name: marin county california coupled fire communication and traffic modelling of wildfire evacuation

description: This case study builds a framework that couples a fire spread model, a model of how evacuation warnings reach people through several channels with different reaction times, and an agent-based spatial-queue traffic model, and applies it to three communities in Marin County, California. The authors, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and Korea University, published it in an open-access journal article. The analysis looks at macro, meso and micro scales, testing how warning timing, background traffic and everyday trips such as picking up children affect evacuation. Coverage is three wildland-urban interface communities in one county. The article is free to read through the publisher's open access copy under the publisher's terms. Caveats: scenarios are simulated, not observed evacuations, and results depend on assumed behaviour and communication delays. The study found that evacuation efficiency depends on warning timing and coordination, that cognitive delays produce non-linear congestion, that peak background traffic reduces capacity, and that local demographic and road network features make evacuation capacity an unevenly distributed form of access to safety. Simulation uses: an example of coupling hazard, communication and traffic models for emergency evacuation planning. Related records: the Chimney Tops 2 fire household survey (case_study-chimney-tops-2-fire-evacuation-household-survey) gives observed evacuation behaviour for comparison.
